countries.name: Afghanistan
countries.line: Health services rely heavily on donor-funded NGOs under the Taliban authorities. Aid cuts and restrictions on women are shrinking care: WHO warns about 10% of Afghans could lose access to healthcare by the end of 2026.

countries.name: Albania
countries.line: Mainly public system financed through compulsory insurance and the state budget, run by the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare. Cancer care, hospital restructuring and medicines funding top the 2026 agenda.

countries.name: Algeria
countries.line: Largely public, free-at-the-point-of-use health system with social security covering most of the population. The health ministry's agenda in 2026 includes cancer control, domestic vaccine production and occupational health.

countries.name: Angola
countries.line: Mainly public, tax-funded system that has expanded fast: 743 health units built in eight years. The ministry is recruiting thousands of health workers, building hospitals and introducing a malaria vaccine.

countries.name: Argentina
countries.line: Three-part system of public hospitals, union-run social insurance funds (obras sociales) and private prepaid plans. The Milei government has cut and merged health bodies, confirmed Argentina's exit from WHO and announced a reform of the health system.

countries.name: Armenia
countries.line: Armenia is moving from a mostly out-of-pocket model toward mandatory universal health insurance, which started in phases on 1 January 2026. Main challenges are heavy private spending, limited public funding, and whether costs stay affordable as projections rise for 2027. Life expectancy is about 77 years.

countries.name: Austria
countries.line: Solidarity-based social insurance system delivering good care, but with long waiting times, high private costs and a growing two-tier risk. Many specialists now work outside public insurance, and budget pressure is driving a federal-state reform push.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
countries.line: Mandatory health insurance rolled out nationwide since 2021. In 2026 control of it moved to the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection, and co-financing by patients was postponed to 2027.

countries.name: Bangladesh
countries.line: Mixed public and private system with heavy out-of-pocket spending (about 79%) and health spending near 2% of GDP. Main challenges include maternal and child mortality, weak immunisation, and a 2026 measles outbreak that killed children. Government is now expanding primary care.

countries.name: Belarus
countries.line: State-run, tax-funded health system inherited from the Soviet model. The government adopted a new state programme, Healthy Nation, for 2026–2030, and is building a centralised electronic health record system.

countries.name: Belgium
countries.line: Health insurance and budgets are central to policy. Costs are rising as the population ages, so the government is pushing efficiency measures alongside extra spending. A new five-year WHO partnership targets accessible, resilient services, and youth nicotine use is a current focus.

countries.name: Benin
countries.line: Mixed public-private system expanding health insurance through the ARCH programme, starting with the poorest. A National Health Development Plan 2026–2030 was validated, and the government funds free lifesaving emergency care.

countries.name: Bolivia
countries.line: Public Single Health System (SUS) alongside social security funds, described by the government as near collapse. The new government's National Health Plan 2026–2030 centres on primary care and integrated health networks.

countries.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
countries.line: Decentralised system: two entities plus Brčko District, with 14 health ministries and 13 insurance funds, which makes reform complex. Social health insurance is mandatory but not universal, out-of-pocket payments are high, and primary care reform is under way.

countries.name: Botswana
countries.line: Tax-funded public system long seen as strong in the region, now in crisis as falling diamond revenues hit public finances. A public health emergency over medicine shortages has been in place since August 2025.

countries.name: Bulgaria
countries.line: Health infrastructure, staff shortages, hospital management and outpatient care development are the main challenges, according to the health minister. Administrative restructuring of health bodies is now being debated, and healthcare-associated infections remain a concern flagged by the OECD.

countries.name: Burkina Faso
countries.line: Public system under strain from insecurity in much of the country. Universal health insurance benefits started in February 2026, and the government reports a 32% drop in malaria cases in 2025.

countries.name: Burundi
countries.line: Largely public system with free care for children under five and pregnant women, heavily supported by partners. Burundi eliminated trachoma and validated a national community health strategy.

countries.name: Cabo Verde
countries.line: Public national health service across nine inhabited islands, with complex cases evacuated to Portugal. The country plans a new national hospital and its first kidney transplant.

countries.name: Cambodia
countries.line: Mixed public-private system with high out-of-pocket spending. The Health Equity Fund pays for care for poor households, and the government is working towards universal health coverage through strategic purchasing.

countries.name: Cameroon
countries.line: Mixed system with high out-of-pocket spending. Universal health coverage (CSU) has been rolled out in phases since 2023 with a mixed record, and a new National Health Development Plan runs 2026–2030.

countries.name: Central African Republic
countries.line: One of the weakest health systems in the world, largely run with humanitarian partners after years of conflict. A cholera outbreak was declared in 2026, and the country is preparing for possible spread of Ebola from neighbouring DR Congo.

countries.name: Chad
countries.line: Public system with 207 hospitals and 2,033 health centres for a large, mostly rural population and many refugees. Dengue, guinea worm and malnutrition are recurring challenges.

countries.name: Chile
countries.line: Dual system of public insurer FONASA and private ISAPREs. The Kast government took office in March 2026 facing long waiting lists, and declared a health alert to clear more than 27,000 delayed cancer treatments.

countries.name: Congo
countries.line: Public system with large gaps between Brazzaville, Pointe-Noire and rural areas. Recent cholera outbreaks and a National Health Council have pushed governance reforms and improvements at the main referral hospital.

countries.name: Costa Rica
countries.line: Universal social insurance through the CCSS, long a regional model, now strained by long waiting lists and specialist shortages. The new government kept the CCSS leadership and changed the health ministry; a CCSS plan aims to cut waiting lists by 2030.

countries.name: Croatia
countries.line: Insurance-based system run through the Croatian Health Insurance Fund. The EU's country health profile names the organisation of care as Croatia's main health-system challenge; waiting lists for diagnostics are a political focus.

countries.name: Cuba
countries.line: State-run, free universal system long known for its doctor numbers and medical diplomacy. In 2026 the health minister said the system was at the brink of collapse because of fuel shortages under the US blockade, with severe medicine shortages.

countries.name: Cyprus
countries.line: Universal coverage through GeSY, the general health system launched in 2019, now with more than one million beneficiaries. Nursing shortages, public hospital capacity and delays in treatment abroad are current pressure points.

countries.name: Czechia
countries.line: Statutory health insurance system with several insurance funds. The new government's health ministry is putting primary care, prevention and system modernisation first, and has agreed a new cooperation plan with WHO.

countries.name: Côte d'Ivoire
countries.line: Mixed public-private system building universal health coverage (CMU) through mandatory enrolment. The government aims for 30 million people enrolled in 2026 and is now focused on turning enrolment into actual coverage.

countries.name: Denmark
countries.line: Denmark has a publicly funded, largely decentralised system in which local governments deliver most care while central government sets goals and rules. Main challenges include an ageing population, rising chronic disease and an imbalance between hospitals and local services. Ida Auken took over the health portfolio…

countries.name: Djibouti
countries.line: Small public system centred on the capital, supported by French and other partners. A health system strengthening project with AFD and new emergency and radiology facilities in the regions are under way.

countries.name: Dominican Republic
countries.line: Mixed system with a national health insurance (SeNaSa) and expanding public hospital network. The Dominican health minister presided over the 79th World Health Assembly in 2026.

countries.name: Ecuador
countries.line: Fragmented system of the Ministry of Public Health and the social security institute IESS. Chronic medicine shortages in public hospitals and corruption cases have led to frequent changes of health minister.

countries.name: El Salvador
countries.line: Public Ministry of Health network alongside the social security institute ISSS. The government is investing in hospitals and telemedicine through the Doctor SV platform.

countries.name: Eritrea
countries.line: State-run public system with little independent information. Government reporting highlights high use of health facilities and maternity waiting rooms that bring mothers closer to skilled birth care.

countries.name: Estonia
countries.line: Single-payer system run by the Estonian Health Insurance Fund (Tervisekassa), financed mainly by payroll tax. The fund has run deficits for years, and how to fund healthcare sustainably is the central policy debate.

countries.name: Eswatini
countries.line: Public system with very high HIV prevalence but strong HIV progress, recognised as a global leader. Medicine shortages in public facilities are a public complaint, and Eswatini signed a $195 million health pact with the US.

countries.name: Finland
countries.line: Public health and social services have been run since 2023 by wellbeing services counties instead of municipalities. An interim evaluation finds the reform progressing but in need of corrections to meet its goals, including cost control.

countries.name: Gabon
countries.line: Public system with health insurance (CNAMGS) and run-down hospitals, especially outside Libreville. The health ministry's reform plan targets dilapidated hospitals, missing specialists, better patient reception and fairer access across regions.

countries.name: Gambia
countries.line: Small public system with high maternal mortality: 130 maternal deaths were recorded in 2025. Falling immunisation coverage and health workforce gaps are current concerns.

countries.name: Georgia
countries.line: State-funded Universal Healthcare Programme with mostly private providers; the minister says over 95% of people have access to state-funded services. A full primary healthcare reform starts in 2026, and registration rules for citizens abroad have been tightened.

countries.name: Ghana
countries.line: Ghana runs a tax-funded National Health Insurance Scheme, which the President says covers about 76% of people. Main challenges are infectious diseases, malnutrition and rising non-communicable diseases. In 2026 Ghana rejected a proposed US health agreement, citing health sovereignty and domestic financing.

countries.name: Greece
countries.line: Universal National Health System (ESY) shifting from hospital-centred care toward prevention and primary care. Main challenges: appointment delays, limited access to contracted doctors, private consultation costs, weak quality data. Notable now: digital and AI-enabled reforms, including a Quality-for-All pilot since…

countries.name: Guatemala
countries.line: Underfunded public system with large gaps for the rural and Indigenous population. The health ministry's focus is rebuilding the hospital network, primary care and an evidence-based 2026 spending plan.

countries.name: Guinea
countries.line: Public system rebuilding after Ebola, with a large share of care paid out of pocket. European partners launched two major programmes in support of the health system, and a national cancer plan runs 2026–2030.

countries.name: Guinea-Bissau
countries.line: Fragile public system heavily dependent on partners, with many patients referred to Portugal. A new health minister promised better services; malaria vaccination has started.

countries.name: Haiti
countries.line: A health system collapsing under gang violence: hospitals in Port-au-Prince have closed or been attacked, and medical groups have withdrawn. Cholera has resurged and WHO has issued a health emergency appeal for 2026.

countries.name: Honduras
countries.line: Public Health Secretariat (SESAL) alongside the social security institute IHSS, in a deep crisis of hospitals and medicines. The new president, Nasry Asfura, took charge of the Health Secretariat himself in January 2026.

countries.name: Hungary
countries.line: Single-payer system run by the National Health Insurance Fund (NEAK). The Tisza government that took office in May 2026 has a new health ministry and promises serious changes to the system.

countries.name: Iran
countries.line: Public health networks under the Ministry of Health and Medical Education, with broad insurance coverage but high out-of-pocket costs and unpaid debts. The 2026 war with the US and Israel included attacks on health facilities, and the government frames the health system as a pillar of national resilience.

countries.name: Iraq
countries.line: Mainly public, tax-funded system rebuilding after decades of conflict, with large gaps in hospitals and medicines. The ministry is introducing digital health insurance and new hospitals; viral haemorrhagic fevers recur each year.

countries.name: Ireland
countries.line: Tax-funded public system run by the Health Service Executive (HSE) alongside a large private insurance sector. Sláintecare, the long-term reform towards universal care, frames policy; long waiting lists remain the main political problem.

countries.name: Israel
countries.line: Universal coverage runs through health maintenance organizations and a national benefits basket. Main challenges include obesity, with over half of adults overweight or obese, and delayed diagnosis in women's care. Wartime pressure is notable: a hospital ward was set up in an underground parking area.

countries.name: Italy
countries.line: Shared governance: the Ministry of Health works with the Regions on prevention and planning. Main challenges include mental health and prevention, and the government is now implementing a 2025–2030 mental health plan and a 2026–2031 prevention plan.

countries.name: Jamaica
countries.line: Tax-funded public system run through four Regional Health Authorities, with a high burden of non-communicable diseases. The ministry is investing in new hospitals and tightening accountability of health bodies.

countries.name: Jordan
countries.line: Mixed system of Ministry of Health facilities, military Royal Medical Services, private hospitals and the King Hussein Cancer Center. Jordan aims for comprehensive health insurance coverage by 2030, and the government insures 4.1 million people for cancer treatment.

countries.name: Kazakhstan
countries.line: Compulsory social health insurance introduced in 2020 alongside a state-guaranteed basic package. The insurance package expanded in 2026, and the government plans to move health financing fully to an insurance model by 2027.

countries.name: Kosovo
countries.line: Mainly public system run by the Ministry of Health, with health insurance long planned but not fully in place. After a year-long political deadlock a new Kurti-led government was approved in February 2026; the government says 171 doctors returned to Kosovo in 2025.

countries.name: Kuwait
countries.line: Free public health care for citizens, with expatriates paying fees and insurance. The ministry has cut medicine prices and tightened governance rules and expat medical checks.

countries.name: Kyrgyzstan
countries.line: Single-payer Mandatory Health Insurance Fund with a state-guaranteed package, but low pay drives doctors abroad. The government is doubling doctors' salaries, building 42 health facilities and testing a new model for state hospitals.

countries.name: Laos
countries.line: Public system with National Health Insurance covering most of the population, but public health spending is low and donor funding is falling. The World Bank's 2026 health expenditure review looks at how to sustain coverage.

countries.name: Latvia
countries.line: Tax-funded health system where state-funded services mainly cover emergencies, and the minister says a funding deficit persists. Main challenges are uneven hospital quality, healthcare funding and pay disputes. Hospital network reform was approved in July 2026.

countries.name: Lebanon
countries.line: Fragmented system dominated by private hospitals, weakened by years of economic crisis. Renewed war in 2026 has hit health care hard: the minister reports 116 health workers killed since 2 March, with public hospitals in the south carrying the burden.

countries.name: Lesotho
countries.line: Public and church-run health system with one of the world's highest HIV and TB burdens, and dependence on South Africa for specialist care. Lesotho completed its second Joint External Evaluation and restructured its health ministry.

countries.name: Liberia
countries.line: Public system rebuilt after the civil war and Ebola, still heavily donor-funded. The health budget was raised to US$110 million, and a new bilateral health agreement with the US has raised concerns about funding cuts and oversight.

countries.name: Libya
countries.line: Health system run by the Government of National Unity; authorities struggle to deliver basic services after years of armed conflict. Main challenges: rebuilding services and non-communicable disease risk, with 44.6% of adults aged 18–69 having three or more risk factors. Recent: Egypt–Libya health cooperation MoU…

countries.name: Lithuania
countries.line: Compulsory health insurance system with a mix of public and private providers. In 2026 new rules favouring public hospitals worried the private sector, and a plan to send newly graduated doctors to rural areas drew criticism.

countries.name: Luxembourg
countries.line: Luxembourg runs a centralised statutory health insurance system with near-universal coverage and free choice of providers, and public funding above 85%. Key challenges are workforce shortages, reliance on foreign-trained staff, and sustainability. Care is shifting toward outpatient settings.

countries.name: Madagascar
countries.line: Underfunded public system with poor access in rural areas and recurring epidemics. In early 2026 a mpox outbreak passed 400 confirmed cases across many districts, and the country trained a national SURGE team for health emergencies.

countries.name: Malawi
countries.line: Free public services alongside the faith-based CHAM network, heavily donor-funded. The new government faces ambulance shortages and stalled hospital projects, and is pushing to eliminate neglected tropical diseases.

countries.name: Mali
countries.line: Public system under severe strain from conflict and the military transition. The government adopted a multisectoral health and well-being strategy for 2026–2035 and a plan to rebuild the health system.

countries.name: Malta
countries.line: Tax-funded public system centred on Mater Dei Hospital, with a large private sector. After the 2026 election the new cabinet put health under the Deputy Prime Minister; hospital projects promised years ago are a political issue.

countries.name: Mauritania
countries.line: Public system with limited capacity outside Nouakchott and outbreaks of haemorrhagic fevers such as Rift Valley fever. In 2026 the government hosted a regional health investment forum seeking private investment.

countries.name: Mauritius
countries.line: Free public health care alongside a growing private sector and medical tourism ambitions. The government wants Mauritius to become a healthcare hub for Africa, and the balance between private care and health insurance is under debate.

countries.name: Mexico
countries.line: Fragmented system of social security institutes (IMSS, ISSSTE) and IMSS-Bienestar for people without social security. The government is building a Servicio Universal de Salud so anyone can use any public institution, with PAHO/WHO support.

countries.name: Moldova
countries.line: Mandatory health insurance system run by the national insurance company (CNAM). The 2026 budget raises funding for compensated medicines and free services; the ministry plans to regionalise hospital services by 2030.

countries.name: Mongolia
countries.line: Public system with social health insurance, facing workforce shortages and a high burden of noncommunicable disease. The government plans large pay rises for health workers and a new NCD action plan.

countries.name: Montenegro
countries.line: Public system financed through the Health Insurance Fund, centred on the Clinical Centre of Montenegro. The government is investing in medical equipment and hospital renovation and aims for equal standards across the system.

countries.name: Morocco
countries.line: Morocco is extending mandatory health insurance (AMO) to the whole population and reorganising care through regional territorial health groups. A new health minister took office in October 2026; overcrowded emergency rooms and regional inequality are key problems.

countries.name: Mozambique
countries.line: Health system organised around a National Health Service (SNS) that depends heavily on donor money. Main challenges: too few health workers and uneven staffing, roughly 92,000 new HIV infections a year, and falling external funding that threatens gains on HIV, malaria, TB and maternal health. The ministry is pressing…

countries.name: Myanmar
countries.line: Since the 2021 coup the public health system has been badly disrupted, with health workers in opposition and conflict across the country. Child vaccination rates have collapsed and international health financing has fallen short.

countries.name: Namibia
countries.line: Two-tier system with public hospitals for most people and private care for the insured minority. Under the 'Vision April 2026' reform senior officials must use public hospitals, alongside investment in infrastructure, staff and ambulances.

countries.name: Nepal
countries.line: Mixed public-private system with federal, provincial and local governments sharing responsibility since 2015. A new health minister, a doctor, took office in 2026 facing a daunting task of revamping the sector.

countries.name: New Zealand
countries.line: Tax-funded public system run nationally by Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora) since 2022. The government has replaced its governance and wants decisions moved closer to communities, with record funding and a focus on patients and waiting times.

countries.name: Nicaragua
countries.line: Free public system run by the Ministry of Health (MINSA) with a strong community health model, and limited independent information. Work with PAHO in 2026 covered digital health, chronic disease surveillance and leprosy elimination.

countries.name: Niger
countries.line: Public system with very high population growth and frequent epidemics, now run under the military government with fewer Western partners. Niger is deepening health cooperation with Algeria.

countries.name: North Korea
countries.line: State-run system with free care in principle but chronic shortages of medicines and equipment. Kim Jong Un has made modernising regional hospitals a top priority, and the 2026 party congress set new public health goals.

countries.name: North Macedonia
countries.line: Compulsory health insurance through the Health Insurance Fund. The ministry changed hands in mid-2026, and the country launched its first WHO country cooperation strategy for 2026–2030.

countries.name: Norway
countries.line: A publicly directed system run through four regional health authorities, with municipal services handling community care. Main challenges: an ageing population, health worker shortages, and poor handovers between hospitals and municipalities. Major reform proposal now in public consultation.

countries.name: Oman
countries.line: Tax-funded public system run by the Ministry of Health. The health budget is close to RO 1 billion, and the ministry is localising services and planning domestic pharmaceutical factories.

countries.name: Pakistan
countries.line: Health is largely devolved to the provinces, with a federal ministry for national health services and coordination. Polio eradication remains the national priority; Pakistan is one of the last countries with wild poliovirus.

countries.name: Palestine
countries.line: Fragmented, aid-dependent system in the West Bank and Gaza, where the Ministry of Health is one of four key providers. Severe financial crisis and medicine stockouts; war damage and displacement strain services. Over a third of essential medicines reached zero stock by June 2026.

countries.name: Panama
countries.line: Split system of the Ministry of Health (MINSA) and the Social Security Fund (CSS), with frequent medicine shortages. The government is integrating MINSA and CSS services into one system.

countries.name: Papua New Guinea
countries.line: Health services are run through Provincial Health Authorities, with very few doctors for the population and high burdens of TB and malaria. Australia, the US and WHO are major partners.

countries.name: Paraguay
countries.line: Split system of the Ministry of Public Health and the social security institute IPS, with recurring medicine shortages. A new health minister took office in September 2026; Paraguay also turned against the new WHO pandemic instrument.

countries.name: Peru
countries.line: Fragmented system with five subsystems: the Ministry of Health (Minsa) covers about 60% of people, EsSalud about 30%, and the armed forces, police and private sector the rest. Poorer groups have less access to care. President Keiko Fujimori's government took office on 28 July 2026.

countries.name: Philippines
countries.line: Universal Health Care law (2019) with PhilHealth as national insurer, but households still pay about 60% of health costs themselves. A new health secretary took over in July 2026; expanding PhilHealth benefits and zero balance billing in public hospitals are current themes.

countries.name: Poland
countries.line: Insurance-based system financed through the NFZ, which an NFZ vice president says is not financially sustainable. Main challenges: waiting lists, doctor pay and staff shortages, plus a 2026 scandal over VIP hospital treatment that prompted urgent reforms.

countries.name: Portugal
countries.line: Tax-funded National Health Service (SNS) alongside private and social-sector providers. Pressure points are emergency departments, surgery waiting times and patients stuck in hospital waiting for continuing-care places.

countries.name: Qatar
countries.line: Well-funded public system run through Hamad Medical Corporation and primary care centres, guided by the National Health Strategy 2024–2030. The government seeks more private-sector participation.

countries.name: Romania
countries.line: Social health insurance system with chronic underfunding and an exodus of doctors abroad. The health minister is pushing financing reform: money following the patient, performance-based pay and a bigger role for outpatient care and prevention.

countries.name: Russia
countries.line: State-run system financed through compulsory medical insurance (OMS) and budgets. In July 2026 the government approved a plan to implement its health development strategy to 2030; replacing imported medicines remains a stated priority.

countries.name: Rwanda
countries.line: Community-based health insurance (Mutuelle de santé) covers most people, with strong community health workers. The ministry is expanding specialist care and hospital beds, and aims to quadruple the health workforce.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
countries.line: Government-led system undergoing structural reform: a Health Holding Company is taking over regional health clusters, separating system oversight from care provision. Chronic disease and injury remain priorities; officials report life expectancy of 79.7 years.

countries.name: Senegal
countries.line: Government-led system with a primary-care focus, where households often pay directly for care. The World Bank notes notable progress over the past decade. A 2025-2034 overhaul of care organisation, hospitals and insurance is now being validated.

countries.name: Serbia
countries.line: Serbia is modernising its health system, with heavy investment in emergency care buildings, equipment and ambulances. Out-of-pocket spending is 32.1% of health spending (2023). EU funding from 2026 targets cardiovascular disease, cancer and youth mental health.

countries.name: Sierra Leone
countries.line: Free health care for children, pregnant women and some groups, in a system still rebuilding after Ebola. A new Health Sector Strategic Plan covers 2026–2030, and the government signed a health agreement with the US.

countries.name: Slovakia
countries.line: Compulsory health insurance with competing public and private insurers. Hospital audits revealed inefficiencies, and the government is reorganising emergency medical services and medicines policy.

countries.name: Slovenia
countries.line: Compulsory health insurance through the national fund ZZZS. A new health minister took office in June 2026 and stresses prevention, access to care and managing the system on data; the future of smaller regional hospitals is a recurring issue.

countries.name: Somalia
countries.line: Fragile, largely donor- and NGO-supported system rebuilding after decades of conflict. Primary healthcare access has risen to about 65% in five years, and a new national health strategy and community health strategy aim to widen it.

countries.name: South Sudan
countries.line: One of the weakest health systems in the world, run largely by NGOs and donors. A new health minister took office in 2026 with a presidential instruction to tackle the health crisis, including cholera.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
countries.line: Free, tax-funded public health system with strong primary care traditions, under financial strain since the economic crisis. A Cabinet-approved reform puts primary care and people-centred services first, with WHO reviewing the reform programme.

countries.name: Sudan
countries.line: After three years of war Sudan faces the world's largest humanitarian health crisis, with many hospitals out of service. Cholera and dengue have spread widely; the government declared one cholera outbreak over, but cases rose again in Kordofan in the rainy season.

countries.name: Sweden
countries.line: Tax-funded system run by 21 regions, with national government setting the frame. Waiting times are the main political issue, and the government is investigating national procurement of healthcare.

countries.name: Switzerland
countries.line: Universal coverage through compulsory private basic health insurance, with premiums paid per person. Rising premiums and costs dominate policy; the Federal Council is pursuing cost-containment packages on medicines, tariffs and deductibles.

countries.name: Syria
countries.line: Post-conflict health system rebuilding under a transitional government. Care relies heavily on out-of-pocket payments, and up to 70% of health workers have left the country. The National Health Strategy 2026–2028 aims to move the sector from emergency response to recovery.

countries.name: Taiwan
countries.line: Single-payer National Health Insurance covering almost everyone, known for low administrative costs. Taiwan is excluded from WHO and the World Health Assembly, which it contests each year.

countries.name: Tajikistan
countries.line: State-run system with high out-of-pocket payments. Compulsory health insurance has been postponed until after 2030; a health financing reform is being piloted in primary care in Sughd region.

countries.name: Tanzania
countries.line: A government-led health system now expanding universal health insurance. Main challenges: high out-of-pocket costs (about 28% of health spending), a shortage of specialists, and expected falls in donor funding for 2026/27. The 2007 Health Policy is under review.

countries.name: Timor-Leste
countries.line: Free, publicly funded health system built up since independence, with heavy reliance on development partners. Timor-Leste eliminated trachoma and hosted the WHO South-East Asia Regional Committee in 2026.

countries.name: Togo
countries.line: Togo is rolling out universal health insurance (AMU), managed by the national health insurance institute and social security fund, with smart cards and a unified digital platform. It invests more in health than its neighbours, according to a 2026 comparison.

countries.name: Trinidad and Tobago
countries.line: Free public care through Regional Health Authorities alongside a large private sector. Dengue and regional disease response are current public health priorities.

countries.name: Tunisia
countries.line: Health system pursuing universal health coverage, with the Ministry of Health aiming for a digital, primary-care-focused reform. Main challenges include recurrent medicine shortages at the Central Pharmacy and pressure on social funds. Notable now: a National Charter for Health signed in October 2026.

countries.name: Türkiye
countries.line: Universal health insurance run through the Social Security Institution, with a large public hospital network and a growing health tourism sector. Current focus is on shorter waits for imaging, prevention (smoking, obesity) and early cancer diagnosis.

countries.name: Ukraine
countries.line: Health system reformed since 2017 around the National Health Service of Ukraine as single purchaser, now operating under full-scale war. WHO has verified more than 3,000 attacks on health care since the invasion; recovery and resilience frame policy.

countries.name: United Arab Emirates
countries.line: Health care is run partly federally and partly by the emirates, with mandatory insurance in some emirates. In 2026 the president directed a national health insurance system for citizens across all emirates and an integrated national healthcare system.

countries.name: Uruguay
countries.line: National Integrated Health System (SNIS) with public and mutual providers funded through a national health fund. Uruguay received WHO's World No Tobacco Day award in 2026 and has legalised euthanasia.

countries.name: Uzbekistan
countries.line: State-run system moving to a state medical insurance model, rolled out region by region and planned nationwide by the end of 2026. Private hospitals can now deliver state-funded services.

countries.name: Venezuela
countries.line: Public health system weakened by years of economic crisis, shortages and emigration of health workers. Earthquakes in mid-2026 overwhelmed hospitals and raised the risk of disease outbreaks.

countries.name: Vietnam
countries.line: Vietnam is moving towards universal health care through social health insurance, which covered about 93.4% of people in 2024. Out-of-pocket spending is still high. Politburo Resolution 72 (September 2025) is driving a shift from treatment to prevention.

countries.name: Yemen
countries.line: A health system split by war between the government and Houthi-held areas, largely kept running by humanitarian aid. WHO says it is at breaking point, with cholera rising and about 20 million people needing health aid.

countries.name: Zambia
countries.line: Public system with free primary care, launching a medium-term health budget and revised national healthcare standards in 2026. Zambia agreed to sign a $1.5 billion health pact with the US after resolving differences over data sharing.

countries.name: Zimbabwe
countries.line: Public system hit by funding gaps, medicine shortages and staff leaving, made worse by the end of US health aid. A new national health strategy, a planned national health insurance and absorbing NGO-funded health workers are the government's response.
